lead: QPSK carries two bits per symbol by choosing one of four carrier phases. It is built from two BPSK signals on carriers 90° apart, so it doubles the bit rate of BPSK in the same bandwidth. M-ary PSK pushes the idea further: with M = 2^k phases each symbol carries k bits, the symbol rate falls by a factor k, and the bandwidth falls with it. The price is a smaller spacing between constellation points, so more power is needed for the same error rate. QPSK sits inside satellite links, LTE and Wi-Fi.
prereq: You need BPSK and its error probability (6.2) and the correlator view of optimum detection from Unit 5, Optimum detection and probability of error in AWGN.

sections.h3: QPSK: two BPSK links on quadrature carriers

blocks.text: A QPSK symbol lasts T<sub>s</sub> seconds and carries two bits, one on each of two carriers. The in-phase carrier is cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) and the quadrature carrier is sin(2πf<sub>c</sub>t). They are 90° apart, so a receiver that multiplies by one of them and integrates wipes the other out.

blocks.where: A is the carrier amplitude in volts, f<sub>c</sub> the carrier frequency in Hz, T<sub>s</sub> the symbol duration in seconds, and I and Q are the two bits in bipolar form, each equal to +1 or −1. The minus sign makes the phase equal arctan(Q/I).

blocks.text: The four combinations of (I, Q) give four phases: (+,+) → 45°, (−,+) → 135°, (−,−) → 225°, (+,−) → 315°. The bits are Gray labelled, so points next to each other differ in one bit only.

items: Split the serial bit stream into two: even-indexed bits go to the I branch, odd-indexed bits to the Q branch.
Convert each stream to bipolar NRZ: bit 1 is +1 and bit 0 is −1, unitless, with any ±1 V levels absorbed into A. Hold each level for T<sub>s</sub>.
Multiply the I stream by cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) and the Q stream by −sin(2πf<sub>c</sub>t).
Add the two products and send the sum to the antenna, after any pulse shaping.

blocks.text: Each branch runs at half the bit rate, so the symbol rate is R<sub>s</sub> = R<sub>b</sub>/2 and T<sub>s</sub> = 2T<sub>b</sub>. With rectangular pulses each branch has a null-to-null width of 2R<sub>s</sub> = R<sub>b</sub>, so QPSK fits twice the bits of BPSK into the same bandwidth. Some syllabi call QPSK 4-PSK.

sections.h3: Coherent detection and bit error probability

blocks.text: The receiver recovers the carrier, multiplies the received signal by cos(2πf<sub>c</sub>t) and by −sin(2πf<sub>c</sub>t), integrates each product over one symbol, and samples at t = T<sub>s</sub>. The two correlator outputs are r<sub>I</sub> and r<sub>Q</sub>. A decision device takes the sign of each: positive → bit 1, negative → bit 0. The pair is then read as the Gray label of the nearest constellation point. Because the carriers are orthogonal, the I decision depends only on the I bit plus noise; the Q branch does not leak into it.

blocks.where: P<sub>b</sub> is the bit error probability, Q(x) the Gaussian tail probability, E<sub>b</sub> the energy per bit in joules, N<sub>0</sub> the one-sided noise power spectral density in W/Hz, and E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> a pure ratio, usually quoted in dB.

blocks.text: This is exactly the BPSK result at the same E<sub>b</sub>, because each QPSK branch is a BPSK system carrying one bit. The symbol energy is E<sub>s</sub> = 2E<sub>b</sub>, and the two branches fail independently, so P<sub>s</sub> = 2P<sub>b</sub> − P<sub>b</sub>² ≈ 2P<sub>b</sub>.

A carrier phase error rotates the received constellation relative to the decision axes and causes I/Q crosstalk; small errors shrink the decision margin, and large errors cause slips to a neighbouring point. Offset QPSK, which delays the Q branch by half a symbol, is covered in 6.6.

sections.h3: M-ary PSK: more phases, fewer hertz

blocks.text: In M-ary PSK the carrier takes one of M phases, 2πm/M for m = 0, 1, …, M−1, all with the same amplitude. M = 2^k with k = 1, 2, 3, …; k = 1 is BPSK, and M-ary PSK usually means k ≥ 2. Each symbol carries k = log₂M bits. The symbol rate falls to R<sub>s</sub> = R<sub>b</sub>/k, and the null-to-null bandwidth of rectangular MPSK is B = 2R<sub>s</sub> = 2R<sub>b</sub>/k. The bandwidth efficiency is R<sub>b</sub>/B = k/2 bps/Hz: 1 bps/Hz for QPSK, 1.5 for 8-PSK, 2 for 16-PSK.

blocks.where: P<sub>s</sub> is the symbol (not bit) error probability, E<sub>s</sub> = k·E<sub>b</sub> the energy per symbol in joules, N<sub>0</sub> the noise density in W/Hz, and M the number of phases. The approximation is good for large M and high E<sub>s</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>.

blocks.text: Adjacent points sit a distance d = 2√E<sub>s</sub>·sin(π/M) apart, so as M grows the points crowd together and each symbol needs more energy to keep the same spacing in noise. With Gray labelling a symbol error usually flips one bit, giving P<sub>b</sub> ≈ P<sub>s</sub>/k. Doubling M adds one bit per symbol and reduces bandwidth per bit by the factor k/(k+1), not by half. Doubling k is what halves the bandwidth per bit. Each extra bit still costs several dB of power.

figure.caption: The four QPSK points at the corners of a square, with Gray labels. Neighbours joined by the dashed lines differ in exactly one bit, so a decision slip to a neighbour costs one bit.

spec.aria: Four QPSK points at the corners of a square with Gray labels 11, 01, 00, 10; dashed edges join neighbours that differ in one bit.

examples.question: A QPSK modem sends a bit rate of 10 Mbps using rectangular (NRZ) pulses and Gray coding. The channel gives E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> = 10 dB. Find (a) the symbol rate, (b) the null-to-null bandwidth, (c) the bandwidth efficiency in bps/Hz, and (d) the bit error probability.
steps: Symbol rate: R<sub>s</sub> = R<sub>b</sub>/k = (10 × 10⁶)/2 = 5 × 10⁶ sym/s = 5 Msym/s, so T<sub>s</sub> = 1/R<sub>s</sub> = 0.2 µs.
Rectangular pulses: null-to-null bandwidth B = 2R<sub>s</sub> = 2 × 5 × 10⁶ = 10 × 10⁶ Hz = 10 MHz.
Bandwidth efficiency: R<sub>b</sub>/B = (10 × 10⁶)/(10 × 10⁶) = 1 bps/Hz, which matches k/2 = 1.
examples.answer: R<sub>s</sub> = 5 Msym/s, B = 10 MHz, bandwidth efficiency = 1 bps/Hz, and P<sub>b</sub> ≈ 3.87 × 10⁻⁶ at E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> = 10 dB.
examples.check:
import math
Rb = 10e6
k = 2
Rs = Rb / k
B = 2 * Rs
eff = Rb / B
EbN0 = 10 ** (10 / 10)
Pb = 0.5 * math.erfc(math.sqrt(EbN0))
print(Rs)
print(B)
print(eff)
print("%.2e" % Pb)

traps: R<sub>b</sub> and R<sub>s</sub> are different. A 10 Mbps QPSK link runs at 5 Msym/s; writing 10 Msym/s doubles the bandwidth you compute.

Use E<sub>b</sub>, not E<sub>s</sub>, in P<sub>b</sub> = Q(√(2E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>)). For QPSK E<sub>s</sub> = 2E<sub>b</sub>, so substituting E<sub>s</sub> makes the answer look about 3 dB too good.
The null-to-null width of rectangular MPSK is 2R<sub>s</sub>, not R<sub>s</sub>. The sinc spectrum has nulls at ±R<sub>s</sub> about the carrier; quoting R<sub>s</sub> as the bandwidth halves it.
In P<sub>s</sub> ≈ 2Q(√(2E<sub>s</sub>/N<sub>0</sub>)·sin(π/M)) the angle is π/M, not π/k or π/2M, and the factor 2 outside is part of the formula.
Gray mapping lowers P<sub>b</sub> for a given P<sub>s</sub>; it does not change P<sub>s</sub>, the constellation or the bandwidth.

quiz.q: How many bits does one QPSK symbol carry, and what is the phase difference between adjacent constellation points?
quiz.a: Two bits per symbol; adjacent points are 90° apart.

quiz.q: Write the symbol rate of M-ary PSK in terms of the bit rate.
quiz.a: R<sub>s</sub> = R<sub>b</sub>/log₂M; for QPSK, R<sub>s</sub> = R<sub>b</sub>/2.

quiz.q: Why is the bit error probability of Gray-coded QPSK the same as BPSK at the same E<sub>b</sub>?
quiz.a: Each branch is an independent BPSK link carrying one bit with energy E<sub>b</sub>. The quadrature carriers are orthogonal, so the branches do not interfere and each has BPSK's error probability.

quiz.q: An 8-PSK link runs at R<sub>b</sub> = 12 Mbps with rectangular pulses. Find the symbol rate, the null-to-null bandwidth and the bandwidth efficiency.
quiz.a: k = log₂8 = 3, so R<sub>s</sub> = 12 × 10⁶/3 = 4 Msym/s. B = 2R<sub>s</sub> = 8 MHz. Efficiency = 12/8 = 1.5 bps/Hz.

quiz.q: A QPSK link has E<sub>b</sub>/N<sub>0</sub> = 8 dB. Find P<sub>b</sub>.
Explain why 16-PSK needs far more power than QPSK for the same symbol error probability.
quiz.a: For M = 16 the angular spacing is 22.5°, so d = 2√E<sub>s</sub> sin(11.25°) ≈ 0.39√E<sub>s</sub>, against 1.41√E<sub>s</sub> for QPSK. Keeping d fixed needs about 13 times the symbol energy, and that energy is now shared over four bits instead of two.

quiz.q: A student says: 'Gray mapping lowers the symbol error probability of QPSK.' Correct the statement.
quiz.a: P<sub>s</sub> is unchanged. Gray mapping only arranges that most symbol errors cross one bit boundary, so P<sub>b</sub> ≈ P<sub>s</sub>/2 instead of being larger.

beyond: Not for the exam. Practical standards rarely stop at plain PSK: π/4-QPSK rotates the constellation by 45° each symbol and appears in mobile radio, while 16-APSK mixes amplitude rings with phase and is used in DVB-S2 because several rings keep points further apart at high M. A recovered carrier can lock 90° or 180° off, and differential encoding or a unique word resolves that ambiguity. Search 'π/4-QPSK', 'APSK constellation DVB-S2' and 'carrier phase ambiguity QPSK'.
